newsitem.title: INDIA: India deeply split over foreign airlines.
newsitem.headline: India deeply split over foreign airlines.

text.p: Usually bitter enemies, Indian communists and Hindu nationalists are up in arms over reports that the government is considering reversing policy to allow foreign airlines to take stakes in domestic carriers.
In April, the centre-left government barred foreign airlines from holding any equity stakes in the domestic aviation sector.
The decision scuttled a proposed $600-million tie-up between Singapore Airlines Ltd and India's Tata group.

It also forced Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways to start planning to sell their 20-percent stakes in private carrier Jet Airways. Jet said on Saturday the government had given its foreign partners until October 15 to sell their stakes.

The controversial policy, engineered by Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, sent tremors through the foreign investment community as it stood in stark contrast to the thrust of the free-market reforms which India launched in 1991.
"There was great disappointment once the Tata-SIA proposal was dropped," said D.H. Pai Panandikar, a corporate adviser to the RPG group. "It is a very bad message for foreign investors."

Now the rightwing opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's communist allies say the Civil Aviation Ministry, in a volte-face, is considering throwing the sector open to foreign airlines.

Gujral, who assumed office at the head of the United Front coalition in April after the aviation policy had been announced, signalled his dissatisfaction with the restrictions during a recent visit to Nepal.
The new prime minister then inducted a junior civil aviation minister in what analysts said was an effort to clip the wings of Ibrahim, who is close to Gujral's predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda.

Last week, BJP general secretary Pramod Mahajan distributed copies of a document which he said proved the government was considering allowing foreign airlines to take up to 40 percent stakes in domestic carriers.

The Communist Party of India (Marxist), members of Gujral's coalition, on Saturday called the 13-page draft policy "a retrograde step harmful for the country's interests". The BJP said the policy was "tailor-made to suit foreign airlines".
Officially, the Civil Aviation Ministry said the government was not reconsidering the cabinet's April decision. But in private, authorities said a review was underway.

"The Civil Aviation Ministry is carrying out an internal exercise to elicit views on various aspects of the new civil aviation policy," a ministry official who asked not to be identified told Reuters.
Analysts said the government's apparent indecision had paralysed foreign investors.
"Good players are shying away because of a lack of clarity in policy," H.K. Malik, chairman of private consultants Konark Aviation, told Reuters.

Nearly a dozen private airlines sprang up after the government ended its monopoly. But most private airlines, weighed down by crippling fuel costs, low passenger fares and government laws that force them to fly to remote, unprofitable regions, are foundering. Only three private airlines are currently flying.

The state-owned airlines are not doing much better. Indian Airlines reported a net loss of 987 million rupees ($27.6 million) between April 1996 and February 1997 following a loss of 1.23 billion rupees in the same period a year earlier.
